# Chapter I.

## The description of the art and the interpretation of alchemy, and what it truly is.

In many and various old books and writings of the philosophers, the description and interpretation of this very art is found quite clearly; therefore, we must also pay attention in this first chapter to that same meaning and interpretation. Concerning this, Hermes the Philosopher <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure considered the founding father of alchemy</note> writes to us and explains it thus: Alchemy is an art of metals, or a metallic art made from one and through one, simply put together, and also a joining together of the most noble things, which overcome one another through knowledge and reality joined or fitted together; and by this same natural mixing, a species of metal is transformed and changed into a better one.

Another philosopher writes thus: Alchemy is an art that teaches how to transform every species of metal, one into the other; and this must happen through its own medicine <note>original: Medicinam; in alchemy, a "medicine" is a substance that "cures" the impurities of base metals</note> or remedy, which is then made clear and written about in many books of the philosophers. And concerning this, it is to be known that alchemy is such an art that is so named by a philosopher who was called and named Alchymus <note>A common medieval folk etymology suggested the word "Alchemy" came from a Greek sage named Alchymus</note>; and the art teaches how to make a medicine, that is, a remedy, which is called the Elixir. This same Elixir, when one throws it upon the imperfect metals <note>Base metals like lead or copper, which were seen as "incomplete" versions of gold</note>, makes them perfect and good: that is the reason for its invention.

---

# Chapter II.

## Concerning the beginning of the metals.

In the words just written, I have fulfilled and completed the first chapter: and now in the second, I will fully explain the beginning of minerals, or the ore of the mines, how and from what they have naturally first sprung and been created. And concerning this, it is first to be noted that the beginning of minerals, ores, or mines is nothing other than <term>Mercury</term> <note>represented in the original text by the astrological symbol ☿</note> and Sulphur, out of which two things all metals are created and born.

Therefore, they are of many and various forms, and are also transformed, some— <note>the text cuts off mid-word "ein-" for the page turn</note>

<summary>This page defines alchemy as the art of perfecting metals through a "medicine" or Elixir and introduces the foundational theory that all metals are composed of Mercury and Sulphur.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Alchymus, Elixir, transmutation, Mercury, Sulphur, imperfect metals, perfection of metals</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the origins of metals, specifically expanding on the "Sulphur-Mercury theory" mentioned on the previous page. It details how the varying purity and proportions of these two principles result in the different known metals.</meta>

...no differently than the other: But Nature always had the intention and set out to make Gold: But the adverse and various accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to external conditions or impurities that interfere with a natural process</note> that occur there make various and adverse metals in transformation, as is then written and found quite clearly in many books of the philosophers. For according to whether the two aforementioned, <term>Sulphur</term> <note>The active, "masculine" principle of alchemy, associated with combustion and color; distinct from common brimstone</note> and <term>Mercury</term> <note>The passive, "feminine" principle of alchemy, associated with fluidity and metallic luster</note>, are pure or impure, accordingly the metals are created or born, such as Gold, Silver, Copper, Lead, Tin, and Iron.

Now to write of Gold: it is a perfect and pure metal, created and born from a pure and fixed Sulphur that is clear and red; it has no defect at all. Tin is an impure metal, and is created from a pure Mercury (which is in part fixed and clear) and also from a Sulphur that is in part pure, clear, and white; and the metal lacks because it is not cooked enough, and it also lacks in its <term>malleability</term> <note>original: Teyung; referring to the distribution of the substance or its ability to be worked</note> and in its fixation.

## Chapter IV.
### Why the Art is to be practiced.

But if you are of such a coarse and hard understanding, and so darkened by ignorance, you will find in the transcribed chapters our true and manifest opinion: specifically, what constitutes the true and right **Matter** <term>original: "Materi"; the starting substance of the Great Work</term> of our **Elixir** <term>The medicinal or transformative substance sought by alchemists</term>. This is also the opinion of all enlightened and wise **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists and natural scientists of antiquity</note>, who place all their focus upon the materials and upon the work of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchymy"</note>. Through this, the Elixir is perfectly completed, so that we may make all imperfect **metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note> perfect. Thus, having now well-recognized this same Material in the chapters, we must make it more than perfect through our masterly work and operation; we must take up and observe its operation and its nature, and thereafter we must direct ourselves accordingly.

We see clearly in the minerals and ores—that is, the **mines** <note>original: "Bergwerck"</note>—that through a constant heat which is enclosed within the mountains, the water therein becomes coarse and thick. Thereafter, over a long time, a **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"; the fluid, "metallic" principle</note> is formed from that same thick water. From the moisture of the earth and through that same **cooking** <term>original: "Kochung"; the process of ripening or maturing a substance through steady heat, similar to digestion</term>, **Sulphur** <note>original: "Schwebel"; the fiery, "combustible" principle</note> is grown and born. Afterward, that same Mercury and Sulphur mix together; depending on whether they are pure or impure, all metals then become either pure or impure. And since Nature now makes perfect and imperfect metals solely through this cooking, why then should we accuse ourselves or venture to accomplish this through other endless and foolish fantasies and the management of our work and operation, differently than Nature does?

Should it be that you wished to surpass Nature and make the metals more than perfect, and wished to accomplish this with a pure regimen and a special operation, such an idea has sprung from a foolish and fantastical head. For God has given Nature a simple, right, and straight path, just like a line, and that happens solely through such warmth and cooking.

You unwise, foolish fools! You do not perceive or know how to follow Nature. Do you not know that the Philosophers say: "this is enough: the **Air** <note>original: "Lus," likely a variant of "Luft" (Air) or "Lux" (Light)</note> and the **Fire**"? They also write: "Warmth completes all things." They say: "cook, and cook yet more, and do not let the cooking vex you." They also say: "Your fire should be blind and moder..." <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "mittelmeſe," meaning "moderate" or "middling."</note>

# Chapter VI.

## Concerning All the Various Colors that Appear in the Work, etc.

Now that you have heard about the **matter** <term>original: "Materi"; the physical substance used in the alchemical process</term> of our **Stone** <term>original: "Steins"; the Philosopher's Stone</term>, and have surely recognized the meaning, the sense, and the path of the work—namely, through which **cooking** <term>original: "Kochung"; the controlled application of heat</term> and governance our Stone must be prepared—you have also seen how it frequently and repeatedly shifts and transforms into various colors during the work. For this reason, it has as many names as it has colors; for the philosophers gave it many names based on the various colors that appear during the process.

For in the first cooking of our Stone, which is called **putrefaction** <note>original Latin: "Putrefactionem"; the stage of decay or breaking down where the matter "dies" to be reborn</note>—that is, rotting—our Stone becomes entirely black. Therefore it is written: "When you find it now in its blackness, you should know that beneath that same blackness the whiteness is hidden; therefore, you must not draw it out, but rather you should cook it subtly until it moves from its blackness into a whiteness."

Regarding this, a philosopher said: "If you find it black now, you should know for a truth that you now hold the first key of the art with true and proper putrefaction." Just as our Stone turns yellow and red—but with the true **redness** <note>original: "Röthe"; referring to the *Rubedo*, the final stage of the work</note>—about which a philosopher writes: "It often turns red and gives itself away; it often flows and often coagulates; and it also turns green before the true whiteness."

Therefore, another philosopher says: "Cook it for so long until the **soul** <note>original: "Seele"; the spiritual essence of the matter</note> appears to you and is born in a green color." And another says: "It dissolves itself, it coagulates itself, and it adorns itself with redness." And yet another philosopher says: "You should know that greenness rules in the greenness; also, before the whiteness, the **color of a peacock** <note>original: "farb eines Pfauen"; a reference to the *Cauda Pavonis* or Peacock's Tail, a famous alchemical stage where the matter displays an iridescent array of colors</note> appears." Regarding this, a philosopher says: "You should know that before the true whiteness, every color that can be imagined in the world will appear."

Afterward, the right and true **whiteness** <note>the *Albedo* stage, representing purification</note> follows and arrives. About this, a philosopher said: "When you have cooked the right, pure, and clear **matter** <term>original: "Setten"; refers to the substance that has "settled" or been prepared</term>—that is, our material—until there appear or are seen within it something like **fish eyes** <note>a traditional alchemical description for the shimmering, small circular spots or crystallization that appear when the matter begins to turn white</note>, then it is ready for work. Then you should know that our Stone is in its **roundness** <note>original: "Rotund"; likely referring to the completion of a circular cycle of distillation and condensation</note> and is ready to be coagulated or made hard."

## Chapter VII.
### Concerning Projection or Tincturing.

And regarding the promise of bringing the perfect and masterly work and labor to a perfect and useful end—that is, the great and excellent **Elixir** <term>original: "Elixirs"; the refined substance capable of transforming metals</term> in white and red: Now it is to be known how the **projection** <term>original: "Projection"; the final step where a small amount of the Stone is "cast upon" base metal to transform it</term>, which is the "casting-on" or **tincturing** <term>original: "Tingirung"; the process of dyeing or permeating a substance to change its nature</term>, shall happen. This is the final labor in this work, for which we have waited and looked forward to with eager joy for a long time; concerning this, we wish to give teaching and instruction.

Now, to speak of the white Elixir: The white Elixir tinctures without end, and it transforms every imperfect metal into a perfect metal—that is, into good, stable, and true silver. Yet it is to be known that one metal is further from, or closer to, perfection than another. And although the Elixir tinctures and makes perfect every metal, it nevertheless tinctures much more easily and better those same metals which are closer to perfection than those which are further from it. And since we now find one metal that is closer to perfection than another, we wish to justify and explain our choice: that we do not need to take the metals that are further from perfection, but rather those that are near.

If you now diligently read through my chapter and consider it well, you will find therein quite clearly and openly which metal is more or less distant from perfection than the others. And without doubt, whoever is of a subtle understanding and rightly notes and understands my aforementioned words will easily find upon which metal this Elixir is to be cast, and from which **matter** <term>original: "Materia"; the raw starting material</term> the Elixir is to be made. ## A Concluding Discourse and the End of this Art.

I have now given you in my aforementioned writings and teaching a pure and perfect treatise; it is named or called a **Mirror of Alchemy**, in which the meaning and secret of the entire art of alchemy appears just as in a mirror. In this, all the Philosophers <term>original: "Philosophi"; the historical masters of alchemy such as Hermes or Geber</term> are in agreement. Because this treatise on the **Mirror of Alchemy** explains and interprets the end [of the work], I was not mistaken to call it a treatise, for it shows itself to be a mirror. Although it is to be studied by itself to learn the art, it hides its face from the uninitiated, yet to the wise, it shows the true art quite beautifully and subtly: just as everyone who looks into a mirror sees and recognizes their own figure, which then looks back at them.

So it is also with the **Mirror of Alchemy**: if one diligently observes and reads through it, there shines forth more than a subtle and beautiful art of alchemy—an art so beautiful, subtle, and also so worthy that it illuminates the understanding of an earnest and refined alchemist, so that he can see the whole truth, naked and uncovered, within it. And out of respect for the dignity of the art, we provide the following figure or symbols <term>original: "Characteres"; symbolic shorthand used to represent chemical substances or spiritual concepts</term> as an aid.

In summary, the **red and the white** <note>The *Albedo* (white) and *Rubedo* (red) are the final two major stages of the alchemical Great Work.</note> alone / is our Stone’s natural food / therein you find the immortal life / that reveals our first son / I love the juice of the vines. <note>A common metaphor linking the "blood of the grape" to the red tincture or the blood of Christ.</note>

### 17.

Let each consider who the Master-Teacher is / it is our dear Lord **Jesus Christ** / the Resurrection alone / the eternal life / Him we should call upon at all times / pray to Him without ceasing / He can give it to you, etc.

### 18.

And if such a thing were easy to find / through **Gold and Silver** alone, or excessively heavy / then even the blind would surely hit upon it / this must happen through the Divine Will alone / if we are to fathom this truth.

### 19.

He who first devised **Alchemy** for us / has made a correct path for many / it happens out of a foundation of true love / with that it shall remain concluded / let the Children of the Philosophers practice themselves therein.

### 20.

We have three Centers before our eyes / the Heavens / Mankind / and the beautiful Earth / therein the **Jewel** lies fast enclosed / he who can reveal this key / he will be quickly admitted into the **Garden** <note>The *Hortus Philosophorum* or the Garden of the Philosophers, a metaphor for the state of alchemical enlightenment.</note>, etc.

### 21.

He who brought such rules together / took heed of Nature’s possibility / secretly found this **Wellspring** / he has also come to the end / the clear Sun shines upon him.

<summary>This page concludes a rhythmic alchemical poem, identifying the Three Principles (Salt, Sulphur, Mercury) and emphasizing that the "Stone" is a gift from God and Jesus Christ rather than a mere chemical product. It frames alchemy as a spiritual and natural pursuit that leads the practitioner to a metaphorical "Garden" of wisdom.</summary>

### Practice

## Regarding the Universal or Blessed Tincture-Stone of the Ancient Sages, composed rhythmically, by an Anonymous Author.

> Pay attention, reader, to what I report to you!
> Here you have a true poem,
> Which I have written for your benefit;
> If you obtain it <note>original: "Bekompst dus," referring to the secret of the Stone</note>, keep it in your guard:
> And do not show it to everyone,
> Let it be entrusted to you alone.
> When you come to the treasure and gain,
> Then throw all apothecary shops away,
> In with the fish into the waters,
> Or in the hog-trough to the swine. <note>A common alchemical boast: once the "Universal Medicine" is found, all standard medicines are considered worthless trash.</note>
> But also be warned alongside this,
> When you wish to begin searching,
> Then go by no other path,
> Than as I will show to you.
> For it is a single way,
> And if you miss that same path,

To think that his own will must be done;
I truly declare to you
That God and human piety may
Withstand the Evil One every day.
For whoever teaches virtue and wisdom,
And turns away evil temptation <note>original: "Anfechtung." Refers to spiritual trials or attacks from the devil.</note>,
Conducting himself with honor and grace,
Living like a human, not like an animal,
And applies himself to truth and justice,
Fighting against unchastity and shame,
He will be quickly raised to honor,
Even were he a child of **Mars** and **Saturn** <note>In astrology, those born under the influence of Mars (war/aggression) and Saturn (melancholy/toil) were thought to have the most difficult temperaments. The author suggests virtue can overcome even the most "unlucky" astrological fate.</note>:
If only, through God’s grace and favor,
You hear me correctly and understand the **Art** <term>the Art</term> <note>Alchemy was known as "The Art" (Ars) or "The Great Art."</note>,
Then I ask you, for God’s sake,
Be also very cautious and very quiet,
And conduct yourself on this earth
Just as I have been taught;
Then God will grant you prosperity,
Temporal goods here, and eternal life there;
For I have truly and freely
Revealed that which was freely known to me:
Not withholding a single letter,
Showing the **Matter**, the **Furnace**, and the **Weight** <note>The three essential components of the alchemical work: the raw materials, the controlled heat, and the precise proportions.</note>,
Together with their preparation;
I cannot tell it to you any better.
If you do not understand it, it pleases me well,
As it is only right that it should be so <note>A common alchemical sentiment: the secrets are revealed, but will remain hidden to the unworthy or the foolish even when read.</note>:

<summary>The author concludes his instruction by emphasizing that spiritual virtue and God's grace are essential for success in alchemy. He claims to have revealed the complete secret of the Matter, Furnace, and Weight, but notes that it will remain hidden to those who do not live a godly life.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the manuscript, following the author's previous warnings about secrecy and the spiritual disposition of the alchemist. It transitions from the physical "Art" of alchemy to a final moral exhortation and a traditional religious doxology, emphasizing that the success of the work depends on the grace of God and the heart of the practitioner.</meta>

Thus my little pearl <note>original: "Perlein." A common alchemical metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone or the hidden essence of the work.</note> remains pure for me,
    And do not worry about making it common <note>Meaning to reveal the secret to the unworthy or the public.</note>.
Although before me there was never anyone
    Who had shown this so clearly to you.
Yet it might still seem too dark <note>Meaning obscure or difficult to understand.</note> to you;
    It should not be entirely manifest,
Lest everyone stumble over it
    Just like a wild bull in a stall.
For I also follow in the footsteps of the ancients,
    As I have learned such things from them:
Not that I set down the **process** <term>process</term> <note>original: "Proceß." The specific sequence of chemical operations.</note> for you,
    Explaining how one should **labor** <term>labor</term> <note>original: "laboriren." To perform work in an alchemical laboratory.</note> at it,
But rather I follow the way of the **Art** <term>the Art</term> <note>Alchemy was frequently referred to simply as "The Art."</note> alone,
    So that I may indicate it to you in this way:
Not so that the sin may be laid upon me
    Because I have moved you to this point,
That I had revealed everything to you
    And thereby endangered myself;
I wish to be held excused of this
    Before God, and let the shame rest with you <note>The author expresses a common alchemical anxiety: that revealing the secret of the Stone to a person who might misuse it is a sin for which the teacher could be held responsible.</note>.
For it is a much different matter [than you think],
    Do not imagine it to be so trivial;
I hope that you will remain **pious** <note>original: "frumm" (fromm). Meaning both devout and morally upright.</note>.
    If your heart is false, may God turn it around
And direct it according to His will.
    With this, my writing comes to an end,
Which I have done for your own good;
    May God keep it in His faithful protection.
To the Divine **Trinity** <note>original: "Dreyfaltigkeit."</note>
    Be praise, honor, and glory, for eternity.
